label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
**The Thursday tea trolley: two of us short**

I came to Wensum Vale in March 2022, eighteen months after I retired from forty-one years of bookkeeping, mostly for a builders' merchant in Dereham. I am not a natural carer. I am not a chatty person. What I have found is that turning up on a Thursday is enough, and that the useful skill is remembering who takes what — which apparently comes in handy after a career in keeping ledgers straight.

Here is the arrangement in full, so you can decide whether it suits you before you commit to anything.

The tea trolley runs in the day therapy unit from 1.30 to 4pm on a Thursday. We are on a rota of one Thursday a fortnight, so it is a half-day every other week. The unit sees fourteen to eighteen patients on a Thursday. Many come for the art group or the hand massage, or simply for the company. Most go home afterwards. We pour the tea, we hand round the biscuits, and we talk to people if they want talking to. That is very nearly the whole job.

At the moment there are four of us on a rota meant for six. Two left over the summer — one moved to Sheffield to be nearer her grandchildren, one had a knee operation. Neither was a falling out with the place, which is the thing I want to be clear about. It is a rota, people move and mend, and this year the arithmetic has gone against us. So we are two short, and Bridget would like a couple more.

If you come along, Bridget does the induction, which takes about two hours, and there is a short food hygiene course to do online. The hospice pays for that, so there is nothing to buy and nothing to pay. Nobody is asked for a DBS check on the spot, or a CV, or a speech about why they want to volunteer. You turn up on the Tuesday, you drink your tea, and Bridget tells you how a Thursday works.

Some weeks are hard. There are weeks when somebody is very unwell and the staff step in and look after us as well as the patients, which was not something I had expected and which I am grateful for. Those weeks happen. Mostly, though, a Thursday is noisy and rather jolly, and I would rather say that plainly than dress it up.

There is a man called Mr Hollis who used to be a signalman. He takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every single week, slightly differently each time. I have stopped correcting the dates. He is not wrong, exactly; he is a version.

My first week I put an entire jug of milk into the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so hard she had to be given a tissue, and said it was the best afternoon she had had in a month. I have not spilt anything since, largely because I am now careful, but I do think about Pat quite often.

The bourbon biscuits always go first. We hide a packet for the late group.

One more thing, and it is the reason I stayed. After I retired I had no regular reason to go out most weeks. I drifted about for eighteen months. Thursdays fixed that. It is not a grand motive and I would be embarrassed to put it in capitals, but it is a real one, and if you are recently retired and finding the weeks shapeless, you will know what I mean.

**If you fancy seeing what it is like, come to the volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm, in the Willow Room.** Tea and biscuits, no obligation, no signing anything. Bridget will be there, along with a few of us who do Thursdays, and you can ask whatever you want. Or ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she will sort something out.

We would rather have two more people on the trolley than a hundred people who read this and meant to get in touch.

---
